The seed differs between the runs, so the rise is only luck

questions.prompt: The seed is set to 42 on two machines, and the scores still differ slightly. What is the likeliest cause?
hints: A seed fixes the sequence of random numbers, and little else.
Library versions and hardware are not controlled by the seed.
questions.onCorrect: Library versions and hardware change the order of operations, so the environment has to be recorded along with the seed.

misconceptions.feedback: The seed is used, but it controls only the random draws. Floating-point order is outside its reach.
Identical results across different software and hardware are not guaranteed, even with the same seed.

choices.label: Identical results are required, so one of the two runs must have failed
The seed was ignored by the model, so its random choices were never fixed
A different library version or hardware, which orders its operations differently

acceptedIdeas: A different library version or hardware, which orders its operations differently
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A different library version or hardware, which orders its operations differently

questions.prompt: A search tries 4 learning rates and 3 depths with 10-fold cross-validation. How many model fits is that, without a final refit?
hints: Count the configurations: 4 × 3.
Each configuration is fitted once per fold.
Multiply by 10.
questions.onCorrect: The 12 configurations each need 10 fits, giving 120, plus one refit on the training data afterwards.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of configurations. Each is fitted once per fold.
That is 3 × 10 and leaves out the 4 learning rates.

questions.prompt: A run record lists the code commit, parameters, seed and metrics. What else must it identify to reproduce the result?
hints: Think of the one input whose change would alter the model without any change in code or parameters.
Which input to training is neither code nor a parameter?
questions.onCorrect: Without the data version nobody can say what the model learned from, and a rerun may silently use different data.

misconceptions.feedback: The author does not affect what a run computes.
The start time helps sort runs, but it does not change what a run computes.
The file size is a result of the run, and it does not let anyone reproduce it.

choices.label: The data version
The size of the saved model file
The time the run started
The author

acceptedIdeas: The data version
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The data version

questions.prompt: A service must handle 300 requests per second at its peak, and each replica of the model can handle 100 requests per second. If the service runs exactly 3 replicas, what happens at the peak?
hints: Work out what three replicas can handle together, and compare it with the peak.
Ask what happens if one replica fails or the traffic bursts.

acceptedIdeas: It copes only while nothing goes wrong, with no room for a burst or a failed replica
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It copes only while nothing goes wrong, with no room for a burst or a failed replica

questions.onCorrect: Three replicas handle exactly 300 requests per second, so they are all at full capacity at the peak, and a burst or the loss of one replica would make requests wait.

misconceptions.feedback: Three replicas at 100 requests per second each handle exactly 300, so every replica runs at full capacity and any burst above the peak has nowhere to go.
Each replica handles 100 requests per second on its own, so three of them handle 300 between them, exactly the peak.

choices.label: It copes only while nothing goes wrong, with no room for a burst or a failed replica
It cannot cope at all, because 3 replicas handle only 100 requests per second between them
It copes comfortably, with room to spare for a burst

questions.prompt: Why is 17.86 replicas rounded up to 18 and not down to 17?
hints: Compare the load each replica would carry with 17 and with 18.
A replica run above the target utilisation answers more slowly.
questions.onCorrect: A fraction of a replica cannot be run, and rounding down would push every replica above the utilisation chosen to leave headroom.

misconceptions.feedback: Rounding down is possible, but it would break the utilisation target here.
Nothing requires an even number of replicas.

choices.label: Seventeen replicas would each run above the target utilisation at peak
Rounding down is not allowed when the result has a fraction in it
An even number of replicas is required so that load can be split evenly

acceptedIdeas: Seventeen replicas would each run above the target utilisation at peak
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Seventeen replicas would each run above the target utilisation at peak

questions.prompt: A peak of 1,000 requests per second, replicas that each handle 80, and a target utilisation of 80%. How many replicas? Round up.
hints: The usable capacity of one replica is 64 requests per second.
1,000 ÷ 64 is just over 15.
Round up to the next whole number.
questions.onCorrect: Fifteen replicas would run at about 83% at peak, over the 80% target, so 16 are needed.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds down. Fifteen replicas would each run above the 80% target at peak.
That is the number at full capacity, 1,000 ÷ 80. The target utilisation adds headroom.

questions.prompt: The peak load is 400 requests per second, each replica handles 50 requests per second, and the target utilisation is 80%. How many replicas are needed?
hints: The usable capacity of one replica is 50 × 0.8.
Divide the peak load by that capacity.
The result is a whole number.
questions.onCorrect: Ten replicas carry the peak with 20% of each replica spare.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number at full capacity, 400 ÷ 50. The target utilisation adds headroom.
That divides by 50 × 0.64. Utilisation multiplies the capacity once.

questions.prompt: Which release step compares a new model on live traffic without affecting any user?
hints: Ask which stage never returns the candidate's answers to users.
Ask which stage exposes users to the candidate's answers and which does not.
questions.onCorrect: In a shadow deployment the candidate sees real requests, and only its logged answers are compared, so no user receives them.

misconceptions.feedback: A canary does return the candidate's answers to a share of users, 50% here, so a fault would reach them.
A full rollout sends every user the candidate's answers.
Retraining builds a model. It does not compare one on live traffic.

choices.label: Shadow deployment
Retraining the model
Canary at 50% of traffic
Full rollout to all users

acceptedIdeas: Shadow deployment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shadow deployment

questions.prompt: A measure of drift compares the share of live rows in each bin with the share seen in training. If the live shares equal the training shares in every bin, what should the measure report?
hints: Ask what each bin contributes when its live share equals its training share.
Each term has a factor (a − e), which is 0 when a equals e.

acceptedIdeas: Zero, since nothing has moved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero, since nothing has moved

questions.onCorrect: The population stability index adds up a term per bin, and each term is 0 when the live share equals the training share, so the total is 0.

misconceptions.feedback: Live data often differs a little in practice, but here the shares are equal in every bin, so there is no difference left for the measure to report.
Each bin contributes according to how far its share has moved, and when no share has moved every bin contributes nothing, however many bins there are.

choices.label: A small positive value, since live data always differs a little
Zero, since nothing has moved
A value that depends on how many bins there are

questions.prompt: In training two bins hold 0.7 and 0.3 of the rows, and live they hold 0.6 and 0.4. What is the PSI to three decimal places?
hints: The first term is (0.6 − 0.7) × ln(0.6 ÷ 0.7).
The second term is (0.4 − 0.3) × ln(0.4 ÷ 0.3).
Both terms are positive. Add them.
questions.onCorrect: The PSI of 0.044 is below the conventional 0.1, so this shift is small.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the conventional alarm level, not the PSI of these shares.
That adds the absolute shifts, 0.1 + 0.1. The PSI weights each shift by ln(a ÷ e).

questions.prompt: A new camera makes every product photo brighter, but a bright photo of a shoe is still a shoe. Which kind of change is this?
hints: Ask whether the inputs changed, the meaning of the inputs, or the timing of the labels.
A bright photo of a shoe still has the same label.

acceptedIdeas: Data drift
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Data drift

questions.onCorrect: The inputs shifted while their meaning for the label held, which is data drift and is caught by comparing input distributions.

misconceptions.feedback: Concept drift is a change in what the inputs mean for the label. A brighter shoe is still a shoe, so the meaning has not changed, only the inputs have.
Label delay is about when labels arrive, and nothing here changes the timing of the labels.

choices.label: Data drift
Label delay
Concept drift

questions.prompt: The expected shares are 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 and the actual shares are 0.4, 0.3 and 0.3. What is the PSI to three decimal places?
hints: The first term is (0.4 − 0.5) × ln(0.4 ÷ 0.5), and the second is zero.
The third term is (0.3 − 0.2) × ln(0.3 ÷ 0.2).
Add the three terms.
questions.onCorrect: A PSI of 0.063 is below the conventional 0.1, so this shift would not raise an alarm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the conventional alarm level, not the PSI of these shares.
That adds the absolute shifts, 0.1 + 0 + 0.1. The PSI weights each by ln(a ÷ e).

questions.prompt: A model selects 40% of group A and 40% of group B, so demographic parity holds exactly. Among the people who deserved a positive decision, it finds 90% in group A and 60% in group B. What does this show?
hints: Selection rate counts everyone selected, while true positive rate looks only at the people who deserved it.
Compare what each of the two measures divides by.

acceptedIdeas: Groups are treated equally on selection rate and unequally on true positive rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Groups are treated equally on selection rate and unequally on true positive rate

questions.onCorrect: Parity on selection rate holds while the true positive rates differ by 0.9 − 0.6 = 0.3, so a model can pass one fairness measure and fail another.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal selection rates say nothing about who was selected. The model finds 90% of the deserving people in group A and only 60% in group B.
The two groups can hold different shares of deserving people, so the same selection rate can find different shares of them.

choices.label: The figures cannot both hold, since equal selection rates force equal true positive rates
Groups are treated equally on selection rate and unequally on true positive rate
The model is fair, because the selection rates are equal in both groups

questions.prompt: What is the name of the document that records a model's intended use, data and per-group metrics?
hints: Its sections were proposed by Mitchell and colleagues in 2019.
It has sections for intended use, evaluation data and results for each group.
questions.onCorrect: A model card travels with a model and tells a new user what it is for, what it was built from and how it performs across groups.

misconceptions.feedback: A datasheet describes a dataset. The document for a model has a different name.
A README describes software, and rarely holds per-group metrics.

acceptedIdeas: model card
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: model card

questions.prompt: Why does computing a true positive rate for each group belong to Measure?
hints: Measure analyses and tracks risks with metrics.
The task computes a rate for each group, which is a metric.
questions.onCorrect: Measure covers the analysis, assessment and tracking of risks, which is what per-group metrics do.

misconceptions.feedback: Setting policy is Govern, which applies across all the functions.
Deciding which risks to prioritise and accept is Manage.

choices.label: It analyses and tracks a risk that has already been identified
It sets out the policies and roles of the whole organisation
It decides which risks are worth accepting and acts on them

acceptedIdeas: It analyses and tracks a risk that has already been identified
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It analyses and tracks a risk that has already been identified

questions.prompt: Which AI RMF function does 'record the training data and known limits in a model card' belong to?
hints: Think of the function that establishes the context and identifies the risks.
Recording the data and its limits describes the context of the system.
questions.onCorrect: Describing the system, its data and its limits establishes the context in which risks arise, which is the work of Map.

misconceptions.feedback: Govern sets the policies, roles and culture across all the functions. A card's entries describe a system and not an organisation's rules.
Measure analyses risks with metrics. A card's descriptive entries set the context first.
Manage acts on risks that have been prioritised.

acceptedIdeas: Map
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Map

choices.label: Govern
Map
Measure
Manage

questions.prompt: In group A, 30 of 40 people who deserved a positive decision are found. In group B, 10 of 20. What is the true positive rate gap, A minus B?
hints: Divide the people found by those who deserved a positive for each group.
A is 30 ÷ 40 and B is 10 ÷ 20.
Subtract B's rate from A's.
questions.onCorrect: Equal opportunity asks this gap to be small, and 0.25 means that group B's qualified people are found far less often.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the counts found, 30 − 10. The gap is the difference of rates.
That is the true positive rate of group B, not the gap.

questions.prompt: After fitting, the four examples are deleted and only w = 1.5 and b = −0.5 are kept. Which of these needs the deleted examples?
hints: A residual is the label minus the prediction.
The model keeps only w and b, so a prediction needs those two numbers and x.

acceptedIdeas: Finding the residual of the student who studied 3 hours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Finding the residual of the student who studied 3 hours

questions.onCorrect: A residual needs the student's actual mark, and only w and b were kept. Every prediction needs just the two parameters.

choices.label: Predicting a mark for a student who studied 2.5 hours
Predicting a mark for a student who studied 6 hours
Finding the residual of the student who studied 3 hours

misconceptions.feedback: The formula ŷ = 1.5x − 0.5 takes any number of hours, so a prediction needs only w and b and not the examples.
The formula accepts 6 hours as easily as 2.5. Whether that prediction can be trusted is another question, but it needs only w and b.

questions.prompt: From w = 0 on the examples (1, 1) and (2, 3), a run with η = 0.6 gives w = 0, 4.2, −4.2 and 12.6 over three updates, and a loss of 5, 19.7, 78.5 and 313.7. What went wrong?
hints: Look at where w goes: it alternates between the two sides of the minimum at 1.4.
Compare how far each w is from 1.4 with the one before.

acceptedIdeas: Each step overshot the minimum by more than the one before
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each step overshot the minimum by more than the one before

questions.onCorrect: At η = 0.6 the distance from the minimum is multiplied by 1 − 5η = −2 at every step, so w swings to the far side and each swing is larger than the last.

choices.label: The gradient had the wrong sign, so w moved uphill
Each step overshot the minimum by more than the one before
The data contain outliers that pull w away from the minimum
The loss is not differentiable, so the gradient is not defined

misconceptions.feedback: The sign was right: the first step moved w up towards the minimum at 1.4 and then past it. The gradient points uphill, and each step went the other way, only too far.
Two clean examples have no outliers, and the same data gave a falling loss at η = 0.1. Only the size of the step changed.
The squared-error loss is smooth, with a gradient at every w. The gradient was computed correctly at each point.

questions.prompt: An email service deletes every message its filter flags as spam, and a deleted genuine message cannot be recovered, while a little spam left in the inbox does no harm. Which measure should the service raise first?
hints: Which measure falls whenever a genuine message is flagged by mistake?
A deleted genuine message cannot be recovered, so which mistake is the costly one?

acceptedIdeas: Precision
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Precision

questions.onCorrect: Precision is the share of flagged messages that really are spam, so it falls with every genuine message that is deleted.

choices.label: Accuracy
Recall
The number of true negatives
Precision

misconceptions.feedback: Accuracy is dominated by the many genuine messages and barely moves when a few are wrongly deleted.
Recall counts how much spam is caught, and here missing some spam is harmless. The costly mistake is a genuine message that gets deleted.
True negatives are genuine messages correctly kept, which says nothing about the ones wrongly deleted.

questions.prompt: A model's AUC is 0.85. What does that mean?
hints: The AUC is defined on pairs of one positive and one negative.
The AUC is not a share of decisions, and it uses no threshold.

acceptedIdeas: A random positive outscores a random negative 85% of the time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A random positive outscores a random negative 85% of the time

questions.onCorrect: The AUC is the share of positive and negative pairs that the scores order correctly, whatever threshold is later chosen.

choices.label: At the threshold that suits it best, 85% of its decisions are right
At its best threshold, 85% of the positives are found
A random positive outscores a random negative 85% of the time

misconceptions.feedback: That describes accuracy at one threshold. The AUC uses no threshold and counts ordered pairs.
That describes the recall at one threshold. The AUC summarises every threshold.

questions.prompt: A model scores 0.62 accuracy on its training rows and 0.60 on its validation rows. What is the likeliest problem?
hints: Compare the two scores with each other, and then with a score you would be happy with.
Which of the two problems gives low scores on both sets?

acceptedIdeas: Underfitting, because both scores are low and close together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Underfitting, because both scores are low and close together

questions.onCorrect: Both scores are low and close together, so the model cannot represent the pattern even on its training rows, which is underfitting.

choices.label: Overfitting, because the training score is above the validation score
Underfitting, because both scores are low and close together
Nothing is wrong, because the gap between the scores is small

misconceptions.feedback: Overfitting shows a high training score and a much lower validation score. Here both are low and the gap is only 0.02.
A small gap alone does not make a model good. Both scores are low, so the model has not learned the pattern even on the rows it was fitted to.

questions.prompt: A model predicts at dispatch time whether a parcel will arrive late, using the columns `distance_km`, `carrier`, `forecast_rain_mm` and `days_in_transit`. Which column leaks the label?
hints: Which column could only be filled in after the parcel has arrived?
Which column is a consequence of the parcel's journey?

acceptedIdeas: `days_in_transit`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `days_in_transit`

questions.onCorrect: The days in transit are known only once the parcel has arrived, so the column exists only for parcels whose outcome is already known.

choices.label: `distance_km`
`carrier`
`forecast_rain_mm`
`days_in_transit`

misconceptions.feedback: The distance is known when the parcel is booked, so it is available at dispatch time.
The carrier is chosen before dispatch, so it is available at prediction time.
A forecast is made before the parcel leaves, so it is known at prediction time.

questions.prompt: A split on loan term sends 8 of the 10 loans to the left child, with a Gini of 0.375, and 2 loans to the right child, with a Gini of 0.5. What is the weighted child impurity?
hints: Each child counts in proportion to its share of the 10 loans.
The left child's share is 8 ÷ 10 and the right child's is 2 ÷ 10.
questions.onCorrect: The weighted impurity is 0.4, so the gain is 0.42 − 0.4 = 0.02. The loan-term question barely helps, and the tree would choose income, whose gain is 0.18, instead.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of the two Ginis. Each child counts in proportion to its share of the loans.
That adds the two Ginis without weighting them. Each child counts in proportion to its share of the loans.

questions.prompt: A tree grown until every leaf is pure scores 1.0 on its training rows and 0.78 on its validation rows. A tree limited to three levels scores 0.90 on training and 0.85 on validation. Which is likely to do better on new rows?
hints: Which of the two scores is measured on rows the tree was not fitted to?
The validation score is the estimate for rows the tree has not seen.

acceptedIdeas: The shallow tree, because its validation accuracy is higher
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shallow tree, because its validation accuracy is higher

questions.onCorrect: The shallow tree does better on rows it did not fit. The deep tree has memorised noise, which is the high variance that bagging averages away.

choices.label: The deep tree, because its training accuracy is higher
The shallow tree, because its validation accuracy is higher
Both about equally, because each fits its training rows well

misconceptions.feedback: Training accuracy rewards memorising, and a perfect score is what a tree that has memorised its examples produces. The validation rows were never fitted, so they are the better guide.
The validation scores differ by seven points, and they are the ones measured on rows the trees never saw.

questions.prompt: The first bin's share fell from 0.4 to 0.3, so (a − e) is negative, yet its term is positive. Why is that?
hints: Work out the sign of ln(a ÷ e) when a is smaller than e.
Look at the sign of each of the two factors.

acceptedIdeas: Both factors are negative, so their product is positive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both factors are negative, so their product is positive

questions.onCorrect: A fall in share makes both (a − e) and ln(a ÷ e) negative, so each bin's term is positive whichever way the share moved.

choices.label: ln(0.3 ÷ 0.4) is positive, because the ratio is a fraction
Both factors are negative, so their product is positive
The difference is squared, so a fall in share becomes positive

misconceptions.feedback: The logarithm of a number below 1 is negative. Here ln(0.75) is about −0.288.
The formula multiplies the difference by a logarithm and does not square it. The product is positive because both factors are negative.

questions.prompt: Two bins have expected shares 0.5 and 0.5 and actual shares 0.3 and 0.7. What is the second bin's term, (a − e) × ln(a ÷ e), to four decimal places?
hints: The difference a − e is 0.7 − 0.5.
The ratio a ÷ e is 0.7 ÷ 0.5 = 1.4.
Multiply the difference by the natural logarithm of the ratio.
questions.onCorrect: The two terms, 0.1022 and 0.0673, add to a PSI of 0.169, in the moderate range of the usual convention, between 0.1 and 0.25.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first bin's term. The second bin has risen, from 0.5 to 0.7.
That is ln(0.7 ÷ 0.5) alone. It still has to be multiplied by (a − e) = 0.2.

questions.prompt: A lender's applicants look the same as last year, but after a rise in interest rates the same income and debt now imply a higher chance of default. Which kind of change is this?
hints: Ask whether it is the inputs that moved or the meaning of the inputs.
Ask whether the inputs look the same but now mean something else for the label.

acceptedIdeas: Concept drift
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Concept drift

questions.onCorrect: The inputs look the same, but what they imply for the label has changed, which is concept drift.

choices.label: Data drift only
Overfitting
Concept drift
Leakage

misconceptions.feedback: Data drift is a change in the inputs themselves. Here the applicants look the same and it is their relationship to the outcome that moved.
Overfitting is a property of how a model was fitted, and it does not come from the world changing later.
Leakage is information from the outcome entering the features, which this is not.

questions.prompt: A lender removes the applicant's age from its model's features but keeps the year in which each applicant first started work. Which statement is right?
hints: Ask whether another column could reveal age.
Work out what the start year of someone's working life says about their age.

acceptedIdeas: The model can still use age, because the start year is correlated with it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The model can still use age, because the start year is correlated with it

questions.onCorrect: The start year stands in for age, so its effect remains, as a name or a postcode would stand in for another removed attribute.

choices.label: The model can no longer treat applicants differently by age
The model can still use age, because the start year is correlated with it
Per-group metrics by age can no longer be computed once the column is gone

misconceptions.feedback: A column that is correlated with age can carry the same information, so differences by age can survive.
The age column can be kept aside for auditing, so per-group metrics by age remain possible.

questions.prompt: A model that predicts flat prices is tested on one flat. The residual, label minus prediction, comes out at −30,000 pounds. What did the model do?
hints: Write the residual as the label minus the prediction, and ask which of the two numbers is larger.
A negative result means that the prediction is the larger number.
questions.onCorrect: The sign gives the direction of a miss and its size gives the amount, which is why squaring the residuals later removes the sign and keeps the size.

misconceptions.feedback: The residual is the label minus the prediction, so a negative residual means the label is the smaller of the two. Predicting too little gives a positive residual.
A residual of zero means an exact prediction. A residual of −30,000 is a miss of 30,000 in one direction.
A residual belongs to a single example. The average miss over all the examples is a different quantity.

choices.label: It predicted 30,000 pounds more than the flat sold for
It predicted 30,000 pounds less than the flat sold for
It predicted the price exactly; the sign is only rounding
Its average miss over every flat is 30,000 pounds

acceptedIdeas: It predicted 30,000 pounds more than the flat sold for
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It predicted 30,000 pounds more than the flat sold for

questions.prompt: A line is fitted to students who studied between 1 and 4 hours, and it is then used to predict the mark of a student who studied 40 hours. What should you make of the answer?
hints: Ask whether any of the four examples is anywhere near 40 hours.
A good fit to the examples does not show the same rule holds elsewhere.
questions.onCorrect: The later lessons on generalisation return to this: a model is judged on examples it was not fitted to, and far outside the range of the examples there is nothing to judge it by.

misconceptions.feedback: The line was fitted only where there were examples. Nothing in the fit says the pattern continues at 40 hours.
A fitted line gives a number for any input, which is what makes a model useful. The question is only whether that number can be trusted.
A small error on the examples says how well the line describes them. It says nothing about an input far outside them.

choices.label: It is as reliable as for 1 to 4 hours, because the same line is used
It goes far beyond the examples, so the fit gives no reason to trust it
It is meaningless, because a model can only predict inputs that were in the examples
It is reliable if the squared residuals on the four examples are small

acceptedIdeas: It goes far beyond the examples, so the fit gives no reason to trust it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It goes far beyond the examples, so the fit gives no reason to trust it

questions.prompt: Two lines are tried on the same two examples. Line A has residuals 2 and −2. Line B has residuals 1 and 1. Adding the raw residuals gives 0 for A and 2 for B. Which line fits better under least squares?
hints: Square each residual before adding.
A sum of 0 can come from large misses that cancel.
questions.onCorrect: Squaring also makes one large miss count for more than several small ones: A's two misses of 2 cost 4 each, while B's two misses of 1 cost 1 each.

misconceptions.feedback: The positive and negative residuals cancel, which hides that line A misses both examples by 2. That is why the residuals are squared before they are added.
Squaring removes the signs, so residuals of either sign can be added and compared.
Direction does not matter once the residuals are squared. Line A misses by more on each example, and the larger misses count for more.

choices.label: Line A, because its residuals add up to 0
Line B, because its squared residuals add up to 2 against 8
Neither, because positive and negative residuals cannot be compared
Line A, because one miss in each direction is better than two in the same direction

acceptedIdeas: Line B, because its squared residuals add up to 2 against 8
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Line B, because its squared residuals add up to 2 against 8

questions.prompt: To fit a straight line to a set of points with the closed form, in what order do you work?
hints: The slope needs two sums, and those sums need the means.
The intercept uses the slope, so it cannot be found first.
questions.onCorrect: The means come first because every later step measures distance from them, and the intercept comes last because it needs the slope.

items: Find the means of the x values and the y values
Add up Sxy and Sxx from the distances to the means
Divide Sxy by Sxx to get the slope w
Use the means and w to get the intercept b
Check the residuals of the fitted line

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Find the means first, then Sxy and Sxx from the distances to them, then w = Sxy ÷ Sxx, then b = ȳ − w·x̄, and finally look at the residuals.

questions.prompt: On the examples (1, 1) and (2, 3) the gradient of the loss at w = 2 is +3. Which way should the next update move w?
hints: The update is w minus η times the gradient.
A positive gradient means the loss rises to the right of this point.
questions.onCorrect: A positive gradient puts w to the right of the minimum, which here is near 1.4, and subtracting it moves w left, towards the minimum.

misconceptions.feedback: A positive gradient means the loss rises as w increases. The loss is falling in the direction opposite to the gradient.
The minimum is where the gradient is 0. A gradient of +3 means the loss is still sloping.
The update subtracts η times the gradient. Adding it would climb the loss instead of descending.

choices.label: Down, because the loss rises as w increases at this point
Up, because a positive gradient means the loss is falling
Nowhere, because any gradient that is not zero is already the minimum
Up, because the update adds the gradient to w

acceptedIdeas: Down, because the loss rises as w increases at this point
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Down, because the loss rises as w increases at this point

questions.prompt: On the examples (1, 1) and (3, 3) the loss is smallest at w = 1, and the gradient at w = 0 is −10. One update with η = 0.25 gives w = 2.5, and the loss goes from 5 to 11.25. What does this show?
hints: Compare the loss before and after the update.
Work out how far w = 2.5 is from the minimum at 1, and how far w = 0 was.
questions.onCorrect: For these examples the safe learning rate is below 2 ÷ Σxᵢ² = 0.2, so η = 0.25 overshoots by more each time.

misconceptions.feedback: The gradient at w = 0 is correct, 1·(0 − 1) + 3·(0 − 3) = −10. It is the step that carried w past the minimum.
The direction was right, but the loss rose from 5 to 11.25. A step has to lower the loss as well as point downhill.
The update rule is w minus η times the gradient. The loss is used to check progress, not to take the step.

choices.label: The gradient was computed wrongly, because w should never pass the minimum
The step overshot the minimum, so η = 0.25 is too large for these examples
Gradient descent worked, because w moved in the direction that lowers the loss
The update should have multiplied η by the loss, not by the gradient

acceptedIdeas: The step overshot the minimum, so η = 0.25 is too large for these examples
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The step overshot the minimum, so η = 0.25 is too large for these examples

questions.prompt: Gradient descent trains a one-parameter model by repeating a loop. In what order do the steps of the loop run?
hints: Nothing can be computed until w and η have values.
The gradient has to be measured at the current w before w can be changed.
questions.onCorrect: The loop measures the slope, takes a step, and checks the loss each time, so a learning rate that is too large shows up as a loss that rises.

items: Choose a starting value of w and a learning rate
Compute the gradient of the loss at the current w
Update w by subtracting η times the gradient
Compute the loss at the new w to see whether it fell
Repeat from the gradient until the loss stops falling

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Start from a chosen w and η, find the gradient there, subtract η times it from w, check the loss at the new w, and repeat the gradient and update until the loss stops falling.

questions.prompt: Three runs start at w = 0 on the examples (1, 1) and (2, 3), where the loss is 5. After five updates the loss is 1.8 with η = 0.02, 0.105 with η = 0.1 and 282.7 with η = 0.5. Which learning rate would you keep?
hints: Compare the loss after five updates with the 5 it started at.
A learning rate can be too small to be useful and too large to work.
questions.onCorrect: A good rate is found by trying a few values and watching the loss, as these three runs did.

misconceptions.feedback: A step is useful only if the loss falls. At η = 0.5 each step overshoots the minimum by more than the last, so the loss grew from 5 to 282.7.
The steps are safe, but five of them lowered the loss only from 5 to 1.8, against 0.105 for η = 0.1.
A rate above the largest safe value, here 0.4, makes the loss grow at every step and it never falls.

choices.label: η = 0.5, because the largest step covers the most ground
η = 0.1: the 0.02 run is too slow and the 0.5 run diverges
η = 0.02, because the smallest steps are the safest
All three, because the loss must fall eventually for any rate

acceptedIdeas: η = 0.1: the 0.02 run is too slow and the 0.5 run diverges
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: η = 0.1: the 0.02 run is too slow and the 0.5 run diverges

questions.prompt: A screening test for a disease is tried on 1,000 people. It gives 45 true positives, 20 false positives, 5 false negatives and 930 true negatives. What does the 5 count?
hints: A false negative is a negative decision that is wrong.
The word after 'false' says what the test decided.
questions.onCorrect: Those 5 missed cases are what recall measures: 45 of the 50 sick people were found, a recall of 0.9.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the false positive count, 20. A false negative is an actual positive that the test let through.
Those are the true positives, 45. The 5 are the sick people it missed.
Those are the true negatives, 930.

choices.label: Sick people the test sent home with a negative result
Healthy people the test wrongly flagged as sick
Sick people the test found
Healthy people the test correctly cleared

acceptedIdeas: Sick people the test sent home with a negative result
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sick people the test sent home with a negative result

questions.prompt: A fraud filter's matrix has 16 true positives, 8 false positives, 4 false negatives and 172 true negatives. Which counts give its recall?
hints: Recall asks what share of the actual frauds the filter caught.
The actual frauds are the true positives together with the false negatives.
questions.onCorrect: The recall is 16 ÷ 20 = 0.8, so one fraud in five gets through.

misconceptions.feedback: That is precision, which looks at the flagged payments. Recall looks at the payments that are really fraud.
That is accuracy, which counts both kinds of correct decision.
That is the share of honest payments cleared, which says nothing about how many frauds were found.

choices.label: 16 of the 24 flagged payments, 16 ÷ (16 + 8)
16 of the 20 actual frauds, 16 ÷ (16 + 4)
188 of the 200 payments, (16 + 172) ÷ 200
172 of the 180 honest payments, 172 ÷ (172 + 8)

acceptedIdeas: 16 of the 20 actual frauds, 16 ÷ (16 + 4)
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 16 of the 20 actual frauds, 16 ÷ (16 + 4)

questions.prompt: A team is deciding which measure to raise first for each system below. Which measure comes first?
hints: Ask which mistake is worse: missing a real case or acting on a false alarm.
Recall counts the real cases found, and precision counts the flags that were right.
questions.onCorrect: The choice follows what each error costs, which is why one metric cannot serve every use.

items.label: A screening test for a serious disease that is treatable if caught early
items.explanation: A missed case is the costly error, and a false alarm only leads to a second look.

items.label: A spam filter that permanently deletes the messages it flags
items.explanation: A deleted genuine message cannot be recovered, so false alarms are the costly error.

items.label: A fraud filter that freezes an account every time it flags a payment
items.explanation: Each false alarm freezes a customer's account, so the flags need to be trustworthy.

items.label: A scanner that sends flagged bags to a quick second check by hand
items.explanation: A second check is cheap, and a missed item is the expensive error.

items.label: A tool that flags possible cracks in aircraft parts for an engineer to inspect
items.explanation: A missed crack costs far more than an unnecessary inspection.

items.label: A system that bans every account it flags as abusive
items.explanation: A ban on an innocent account is the costly error, so a flag must usually be right.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Recall comes first for the disease screen, the bag scanner and the crack finder, because a miss costs more there. Precision comes first for the spam filter, the fraud freeze and the ban, because a false alarm costs more.

questions.prompt: Two versions of a bank's fraud filter are tried on the same payments. Version A misses 20 frauds and wrongly flags 10 honest payments. Version B misses 8 frauds and wrongly flags 150 honest payments. A missed fraud costs the bank £120, and a wrongly flagged payment costs £4 in staff time. Which version costs less?
hints: Multiply each kind of error by its cost, then add.
A missed fraud costs thirty times as much as a false alarm.
questions.onCorrect: The cheaper filter has the lower precision, since it flags far more honest payments, and it costs less because the errors it avoids are the dear ones.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only one kind of error. Version A's 20 misses cost £2,400, much more than version B's 8.
That counts every error as equal. The two kinds cost different amounts, £120 and £4.
Accuracy treats both errors as one, which is the problem here. The cost of each kind of error is enough.

choices.label: Version A, because it makes far fewer wrong flags
Version B, at £1,560 against £2,440 for version A
Version A, because 30 errors is fewer than 158
They cannot be compared without the filters' accuracy

acceptedIdeas: Version B, at £1,560 against £2,440 for version A
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Version B, at £1,560 against £2,440 for version A

questions.prompt: A fraud model has an AUC of 0.97 on 1,000,000 payments, 1,000 of which are fraud. At the threshold the team uses, it finds 800 of the frauds and also flags 1% of the honest payments. About what share of the flagged payments are fraud?
hints: Count the false alarms: 1% of the honest payments.
Precision is the frauds found divided by everything flagged.
questions.onCorrect: A small false positive rate on very many negatives still gives a large number of false alarms, so the precision can be poor under a high AUC.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the recall. Precision divides by everything flagged, and the false alarms are far more numerous than the 800 frauds.
AUC is a measure of ranking, not of the share of flags that are right, and it uses no threshold at all.
Clearing 99% of honest payments still leaves 1% of 999,000 flagged by mistake, which is 9,990 payments.

choices.label: About 7%, because about 9,990 honest payments are flagged as well
About 80%, because that is the share of frauds it finds
About 97%, because that is the model's AUC
About 99%, because that is the share of honest payments cleared

acceptedIdeas: About 7%, because about 9,990 honest payments are flagged as well
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 7%, because about 9,990 honest payments are flagged as well

questions.prompt: On eight scored examples, thresholds of 0.8, 0.6 and 0.4 give (precision, recall) of (1.0, 0.5), (0.75, 0.75) and (0.667, 1.0). Missing a positive is far more costly here than a false alarm. Which threshold would you use?
hints: Decide which error is the costly one, then read down that column.
Lowering the threshold raises recall and lets in false positives.
questions.onCorrect: Choosing 0.4 accepts two false alarms among six flags to avoid missing any of the four positives.

misconceptions.feedback: Precision counts the flags that were right, and it ignores the positives that were missed. At 0.8 half of the positives are missed.
Balance is not the aim when a miss costs more. At 0.6 one positive in four is still missed.
The AUC summarises the ranking, but each threshold gives a different precision and recall, and the costs decide which to use.

choices.label: 0.8, which has the highest precision
0.6, where precision and recall are equal
0.4, which finds every positive
Any of them, since the model's AUC is the same at every threshold

acceptedIdeas: 0.4, which finds every positive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 0.4, which finds every positive

questions.prompt: Model A has an AUC of 0.91 and model B has 0.89. The team can accept at most 2% false positives. At that rate model A finds 55% of the positives and model B finds 70%. Which model should it use?
hints: Which point on the curve will the team actually run at?
Two curves with different areas can still cross.
questions.onCorrect: The AUC is the right summary before a threshold is chosen, and the precision and recall at the chosen threshold are what the user then experiences.

misconceptions.feedback: The AUC averages over every threshold, but the team will run at one point on the curve. At that point B finds more.
A higher AUC does not mean the curve is higher everywhere. Two ROC curves can cross.
The AUC is a fair summary of ranking when no threshold has been chosen. Here the threshold is known, so the curve at that point matters more.

choices.label: Model A, because its AUC is higher
Model B, because it finds more positives at the false positive rate the team can accept
Model A, because a higher AUC means more positives found at every false positive rate
Neither, because the AUC cannot be used to compare models

acceptedIdeas: Model B, because it finds more positives at the false positive rate the team can accept
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Model B, because it finds more positives at the false positive rate the team can accept

questions.prompt: A model is trained on 100, 400 and 1,600 rows. Its training accuracy is 0.99, 0.98 and 0.97, and its validation accuracy is 0.70, 0.78 and 0.84. What does this suggest?
hints: Watch the validation accuracy as the number of rows grows.
Is the gap between the two scores closing?
questions.onCorrect: A learning curve like this shows whether more data is worth collecting: a gap that narrows with more rows says it is, and two low scores that have already met say it is not.

misconceptions.feedback: The training accuracy is not the one to improve. Validation accuracy has risen with every increase in rows, so more rows are helping.
Underfitting shows as low scores on both sets. Here the training score is high, and the gap is the sign of overfitting.
More rows improve a model that overfits, with no leak needed. A leak would raise the validation score at every size.

choices.label: More training rows should keep narrowing the gap, since the model overfits small samples
More rows will not help, because the training accuracy is already close to 1
The model underfits, because the validation accuracy is below the training accuracy
The validation set has leaked into training, because accuracy rises with more rows

acceptedIdeas: More training rows should keep narrowing the gap, since the model overfits small samples
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More training rows should keep narrowing the gap, since the model overfits small samples

questions.prompt: You have fitted polynomials of degree 1, 3 and 9 and want to pick one of them. On which set do you compare them?
hints: Which set is meant for choosing settings such as the degree?
Which set must stay untouched until the end?
questions.onCorrect: The validation set is used up a little by every choice made on it, which is why a third, untouched test set exists.

misconceptions.feedback: Training error only falls as the model gets more flexible, so it would always pick degree 9.
The test set keeps its value only if it is used once, at the end. Choosing on it makes its score optimistic.
Combining them leaves nothing unseen, so no score would show how the chosen model does on new data.

choices.label: The training set, where the best model has the lowest error
The validation set, which the fitting never used
The test set, since it is the most honest one
All three combined, to use as much data as possible

acceptedIdeas: The validation set, which the fitting never used
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The validation set, which the fitting never used

questions.prompt: Six models are checked on the rows they were fitted to and on validation rows. Which problem does each pair of scores show?
hints: Check whether the two scores are both good, then how far apart they are.
Accuracy is better when higher and error is better when lower.
questions.onCorrect: A gap between the two scores points to overfitting, and two poor scores that agree point to underfitting.

items.label: Training accuracy 0.99, validation accuracy 0.78
items.explanation: A high training score with a much lower validation score is the sign of overfitting.

items.label: Training accuracy 0.58, validation accuracy 0.57
items.explanation: Both scores are low and close together, so the model cannot represent the pattern.

items.label: Training accuracy 0.91, validation accuracy 0.89
items.explanation: Both scores are high and the gap is small.

items.label: Training error 0.02, validation error 0.40
items.explanation: A tiny training error with a large validation error means the noise was learned.

items.label: Training error 0.45, validation error 0.47
items.explanation: Both errors are high and close together, so the model is too simple.

items.label: Training error 0.06, validation error 0.07
items.explanation: Both errors are low and nearly equal.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pairs 0.99 and 0.78, and 0.02 and 0.40, are overfitting. The pairs 0.58 and 0.57, and 0.45 and 0.47, are underfitting. The pairs 0.91 and 0.89, and 0.06 and 0.07, fit well.

questions.prompt: A team predicts next week's electricity demand. It shuffles two years of daily data and splits it at random, and the model's error on the test days is 3%. Used on the weeks that follow, its error is 19%. What is the likeliest cause?
hints: Which days did the model see when it was trained?
In use, can the model see days after the one it predicts?
questions.onCorrect: Splitting by time keeps the future out of training, and the score on the last weeks is a fair preview of deployment.

misconceptions.feedback: Underfitting shows as a poor score on the training rows too. Here the model did well on the shuffled test days.
A small test set would add noise in both directions. A 16-point gap points to something systematic.
The model did well on the shuffled days. The split, not the task, made the test easy.

choices.label: Training saw days on both sides of each test day, so the error was too low
The model underfits, because its error on later weeks is higher than before
The test set was too small, so the error on it was unstable
Demand cannot be predicted from earlier days, whatever the split

acceptedIdeas: Training saw days on both sides of each test day, so the error was too low
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Training saw days on both sides of each test day, so the error was too low

questions.prompt: A model has 200 features, and you suspect that most of them carry no signal. You want a model that uses only a few. Which penalty fits?
hints: Which penalty is built from absolute values?
A model that uses only a few features needs most coefficients to be exactly 0.
questions.onCorrect: The L1 penalty gives a sparse model, which is easier to read and to monitor, while L2 keeps all the features with small coefficients.

misconceptions.feedback: L2 keeps every feature, with a small coefficient on each. It rarely sets one exactly to zero.
Only the L1 penalty reaches exactly 0 at a finite λ. L2 shrinks coefficients towards 0 without switching them off.
A penalty is most useful when there are many parameters to restrain.

choices.label: L1, because it can switch useless features off completely
L2, because it shrinks every coefficient the most
Either one, because both set coefficients exactly to 0 once λ is large enough
Neither, because a penalty only works with few features

acceptedIdeas: L1, because it can switch useless features off completely
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: L1, because it can switch useless features off completely

questions.prompt: Five-fold cross-validation scores λ = 0.1 best of the strengths tried, and the five fitted models are still in memory. Which model do you ship?
hints: What did cross-validation measure: a model, or a setting?
The five models were each trained on only part of the rows.
questions.onCorrect: Cross-validation gives an estimate for choosing a setting, and the chosen setting is then fitted again on all the training data.

misconceptions.feedback: That model saw only four fifths of the rows, and its score reflects one fold. The folds were a way to score the setting.
Averaging fitted parameters is not what cross-validation provides, and it need not give a model that works.
Each of the five was trained on a different four fifths of the rows. None used all the data.

choices.label: The fold model with the highest score, since it did best on its own held-out fold
A model fitted again on all the training data with λ = 0.1
The average of the five models' parameters
Any one of the five, since all five used λ = 0.1

acceptedIdeas: A model fitted again on all the training data with λ = 0.1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A model fitted again on all the training data with λ = 0.1

questions.prompt: Five-fold scores for three penalty strengths: λ = 0.001 gives 0.70, 0.78, 0.66, 0.80 and 0.76 (mean 0.74); λ = 0.1 gives 0.82, 0.80, 0.81, 0.83 and 0.79 (mean 0.81); λ = 10 gives 0.71, 0.70, 0.69, 0.72 and 0.70 (mean 0.70). Which strength would you choose?
hints: Compare the means first, and then the spread.
When the means differ by more than the spread, the difference is real.
questions.onCorrect: The mean says how well a setting does and the spread says how far to trust that figure, so the mean decides unless two settings tie.

misconceptions.feedback: A small spread helps only when the means agree. Here λ = 10 is steady but about eleven points lower on average.
A single fold is the luck of the split. Its scores range from 0.66 to 0.80, so it is both lower on average and less predictable.
The means differ by far more than the spread of λ = 0.1, so the difference is not the luck of the folds.

choices.label: λ = 0.1, which has the highest mean and a small spread
λ = 10, which has the smallest spread of the three settings
λ = 0.001, since one of its folds scored 0.80
Any of them, since the fold scores overlap

acceptedIdeas: λ = 0.1, which has the highest mean and a small spread
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: λ = 0.1, which has the highest mean and a small spread

questions.prompt: A penalised model has its λ raised from 0.1 to 1, which shrinks its coefficients. What happens to its error on the training rows?
hints: Compare the best coefficients with and without the penalty.
The unpenalised fit is the best the model can do on the training rows.
questions.onCorrect: The cost in training fit is worth paying only if the validation error falls, which is why λ is chosen on validation data.

misconceptions.feedback: Shrinking the coefficients moves them away from the values that fit the training rows best, so the fit gets worse.
The penalty is part of the loss that is minimised on the training rows, so it changes the fitted coefficients.
A penalty restrains the fit, and it cannot bring the training error to zero.

choices.label: It rises, because a penalty always costs some fit to the training data
It falls, because a smaller model fits the data more tightly
It stays exactly the same, because the penalty only acts on new data
It falls to zero, because the penalty removes the noise

acceptedIdeas: It rises, because a penalty always costs some fit to the training data
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises, because a penalty always costs some fit to the training data

questions.prompt: A team scores one setting with five-fold cross-validation and then ships a model. In what order do the steps run?
hints: A fold cannot be held out before the data has been cut.
The average needs all five scores.
questions.onCorrect: Only the final fit produces a model to ship, since the five fold models were a way to score the setting.

items: Cut the training data into five folds
Hold out one fold and fit the model on the other four
Score the model on the held-out fold
Repeat until every fold has been held out once, then average the five scores
Fit the chosen setting again on all the training data

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cut the data into folds, fit on four and score on the held-out one, repeat for every fold and average the scores, and fit the chosen setting again on all the training data.

questions.prompt: Training and validation accuracy for three penalty strengths: λ = 0 gives 0.99 and 0.71, λ = 1 gives 0.90 and 0.86, and λ = 100 gives 0.62 and 0.60. What is the problem at λ = 100?
hints: Look at both scores before looking at the gap.
Which λ in the table leaves the model with the best validation score?
questions.onCorrect: The penalty moves a model along a scale from high variance at λ = 0 to high bias at λ = 100, and the best strength sits between.

misconceptions.feedback: Overfitting shows as a high training score with a low validation score, which is λ = 0. At λ = 100 both scores are low.
Leakage inflates a score, and here both are poor. Scores that agree at a low level show a model that is too simple.
A small gap is not enough. Both scores are low, so the model cannot represent the pattern.

choices.label: Overfitting, because the penalty is so strong
Underfitting, because the penalty is so strong that the model is too stiff
Leakage, because training and validation scores are almost equal
Nothing, because the gap between the scores is smaller than at λ = 1

acceptedIdeas: Underfitting, because the penalty is so strong that the model is too stiff
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Underfitting, because the penalty is so strong that the model is too stiff

questions.prompt: A nearest-neighbour model finds the flats most like a new flat by the distance between rows. The columns are floor area (40 to 120 square metres) and number of rooms (1 to 5). With no scaling, which column mostly decides which flats count as nearest?
hints: Compare the size of a typical gap in each column.
Distance adds up the gaps in the units each column is measured in.
questions.onCorrect: Scaling puts the columns on a comparable footing, and the scaler's numbers have to come from the training rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Distance is computed from the raw numbers and knows nothing about importance. A gap of 2 rooms is small next to a gap of 20 square metres.
Distance adds the squared gaps in the raw units, so a column with larger numbers contributes far more.

choices.label: Floor area, because its values vary over a much wider range
Number of rooms, because it is the more important feature
Both equally, because distance treats every column alike

acceptedIdeas: Floor area, because its values vary over a much wider range
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Floor area, because its values vary over a much wider range

questions.prompt: A column holds how a person travelled: bike, bus, car or walk. A team encodes the levels as 1, 2, 3 and 4 and feeds the column to a linear model. What does that assume?
hints: A linear model multiplies the column by one weight.
Does the order 1, 2, 3, 4 mean anything for travel?
questions.onCorrect: One-hot encoding gives each level its own column, so no order is implied, and the set of levels is itself learned from the training rows.

misconceptions.feedback: A linear model multiplies the code by a weight, so it treats the codes as numbers with an order and a spacing.
One-hot columns avoid any order between the levels. Integer codes impose one.
The codes say nothing about how often each level occurs.

choices.label: That a walk is four times a bike, and a car lies between a bus and a walk
Nothing, since the model treats the codes as labels and not as numbers
That the levels are unrelated, exactly as they would be in one-hot columns
That the four ways of travelling occur equally often in the data

acceptedIdeas: That a walk is four times a bike, and a car lies between a bus and a walk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That a walk is four times a bike, and a car lies between a bus and a walk

questions.prompt: A team runs `X_all = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)` on its whole table, and then splits `X_all` into training and test rows. What is wrong with that order?
hints: Which rows did the scaler learn its mean and standard deviation from?
The test rows should not influence anything the model learns.
questions.onCorrect: The safe habit is to split first, fit the scaler on the training rows, and apply the same numbers to the validation and test rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Leakage does not need the labels. The scaler's mean and standard deviation include the test rows, so they influence what the model sees in training.
Scaling is often needed. The fault is where its numbers come from, not that it is used.
`fit_transform` works on any number of columns. The problem is what it was fitted on.

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, since scaling is only arithmetic and uses none of the labels
The scaler's statistics include the test rows, which leaks them into training
Scaling should be avoided, because it changes the values the model sees
`fit_transform` cannot be used on a table with more than one column

acceptedIdeas: The scaler's statistics include the test rows, which leaks them into training
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The scaler's statistics include the test rows, which leaks them into training

questions.prompt: A service wants to predict on the 1st of each month which customers will cancel during that month. Which columns are safe to use, and which leak the label?
hints: Ask of each column: would it already have its value on the 1st?
A column that only exists for people who cancel gives the answer away.
questions.onCorrect: A score that looks too good is the warning sign, and the test is always the same question about time.

items.label: Months since the customer signed up, as on the 1st
items.explanation: It is known on the 1st, before the month starts.

items.label: The cancellation reason, filled in when a customer cancels
items.explanation: It exists only for customers who cancel, so it gives the answer away.

items.label: Number of support tickets opened before the 1st
items.explanation: The tickets were all opened before the prediction is made.

items.label: A refund issued when a customer cancels
items.explanation: A refund follows a cancellation, so it is a consequence of the label.

items.label: Whether the customer opened the app in the last week of the previous month
items.explanation: It happened before the 1st.

items.label: Days between the 1st and the customer's final login
items.explanation: Only a customer who leaves has a final login, and it is known after the 1st.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Months since signup, tickets before the 1st and last week's app use are known on the 1st. The cancellation reason, the refund and the days to the final login are only known after the outcome.

questions.prompt: A team scales all its rows, then runs 5-fold cross-validation and gets 0.93. On genuinely new data the model scores 0.88. Which change gives a fairer cross-validation score?
hints: Where did the scaler learn its numbers?
In each round, which rows are meant to be unseen?
questions.onCorrect: A pipeline refits every step on the training folds of each round, so the held-out fold stays untouched.

misconceptions.feedback: The fault is that the scaler saw every fold before the rounds began. More folds leave that unchanged.
The held-out rows would then shape the scaler, which is the leak again.
A scaler leaks only when it is fitted on rows that should be unseen. Fitted inside each round, it is safe.

choices.label: Use a pipeline, so the scaler is refitted on the training folds of each round
Use more folds, so that each held-out fold is smaller and the scores are steadier
Scale after cross-validation, using the held-out folds' statistics
Drop the scaler, since every scaler leaks

acceptedIdeas: Use a pipeline, so the scaler is refitted on the training folds of each round
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use a pipeline, so the scaler is refitted on the training folds of each round

questions.prompt: Three nodes hold 10 loans each. Node X has 9 repaid and 1 unpaid, node Y has 5 and 5, and node Z has 7 and 3. Which has the lowest Gini impurity?
hints: Impurity is lowest when almost every example belongs to one class.
A pure node has an impurity of 0.
questions.onCorrect: The three impurities are 0.18, 0.50 and 0.42, so X is the cleanest and Y the most mixed.

misconceptions.feedback: A balanced node is the most mixed possible, with the largest impurity, 0.5.
Z has an impurity of 0.42, which is between the others and not the lowest.

choices.label: Node Y, because its two classes are balanced
Node X, because it is mostly one class
Node Z, because it sits between the other two

Why does a vote of many trees help only if the trees differ?
flashcards.back: Identical trees make identical errors, so the majority is no better than one tree, while different trees make different errors that the vote outvotes.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the function, such as ReLU or sigmoid, that a neuron applies to its weighted sum?
flashcards.back: Without an activation, stacked layers would reduce to a single linear map.

acceptedIdeas: activation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: activation

flashcards.front: A layer has 6 inputs and 4 neurons, with a bias on each neuron. How many parameters does it have?
flashcards.back: The layer has 6 × 4 weights and 4 biases: 24 + 4 = 28.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The layer has 6 × 4 weights and 4 biases: 24 + 4 = 28.

flashcards.front: Why is an activation needed between layers?
flashcards.back: Without one, the layers multiply out to a single linear map, so extra layers add no power.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a fingerprint computed from the bytes of a file, used to identify a dataset in a run record?
flashcards.back: A hash changes completely if any byte changes, so it detects data that was altered.

acceptedIdeas: hash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: hash

flashcards.front: Two runs share a commit, a seed and every parameter, and their scores differ. Which field of the run records should you compare next?
flashcards.back: The data hash. The same code and settings on different data can give different scores, and only the hash shows that the data changed.

acceptedIdeas: data hash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: data hash

flashcards.front: Why is saving the model file not enough to reproduce a result?
flashcards.back: Without the code commit, the data version, the parameters, the seed and the environment, nobody can say what the model learned from or rebuild it.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a release stage in which a candidate model receives a copy of live traffic but its answers are never returned to users?
flashcards.back: A shadow deployment compares a candidate with the current model on real requests while no user sees the candidate's output.

acceptedIdeas: shadow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: shadow

flashcards.front: A feature is measured in days in the training pipeline and in hours in the serving code. What is this problem called?
flashcards.back: Train-serve skew. The model receives values it was not trained on, so the offline score no longer applies.

acceptedIdeas: train-serve skew
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: train-serve skew

flashcards.front: Why is passing offline evaluation not enough to ship a model?
flashcards.back: Production features can be computed differently from training features, and real traffic can differ from the test set, so a staged release has to check the model there.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a change in the relationship between the inputs and the label, so that the same features now imply a different outcome?
flashcards.back: Concept drift makes a model's learned rule out of date even when the input distributions have not moved.

acceptedIdeas: concept drift
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: concept drift

flashcards.front: Two bins have expected shares 0.5 and 0.5 and the same actual shares. What is the PSI?
flashcards.back: With no shift each term has (a − e) = 0, so the PSI is 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no shift each term has (a − e) = 0, so the PSI is 0.

flashcards.front: Why can stable accuracy fail to mean there is no drift?
flashcards.back: Labels may arrive late, so the accuracy shown describes old predictions, while the inputs may already have shifted.

flashcards.front: Which fairness measure compares the share of each group that receives the positive decision?
flashcards.back: Demographic parity asks selection rates to be equal across groups, which ignores who deserved the decision.

acceptedIdeas: demographic parity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: demographic parity

flashcards.front: Two groups have the same selection rate but different true positive rates. Which comparison of the two groups shows the gap?
flashcards.back: Equal opportunity compares the true positive rate, the share of qualified people who are found, so it shows a gap that equal selection rates hide.

acceptedIdeas: equal opportunity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: equal opportunity

flashcards.front: Why does removing a protected attribute from the features not remove bias?
flashcards.back: Other features can be correlated with it and carry the same information, so the model recovers it and the bias in the labels comes through.
